title: Habit anchors
hookLine: B. J. Fogg's Tiny Habits: attach a new habit to an old one
last: A WHEN-THEN PLAN DECIDES AHEAD OF TIME.

cards: The toilet flushes. That's the moment. A Stanford researcher named B.
J. Fogg has described doing a couple of push-ups right after, every time, because the flush was going to happen anyway. He doesn't mind the laugh, but it's a working example of a serious idea.
Nobody has to remember to do the push-ups. The flush remembers for him. An old habit, one that never gets skipped, is carrying a new one on its back.
Today's word is the name for that old habit: the thing a new practice can hold on to.

teach.h: THE ANCHOR: WHAT YOU ALREADY DO.
teach.b: First, the anchor. In his book Tiny Habits, Fogg calls the existing routine an anchor: something you already do reliably, every day, without thinking. Brushing your teeth.
Pouring the first coffee. Turning off the car. The anchor is solid, so it can hold weight.
Second, the recipe: a sentence with two blanks.

After I do this old thing, I will do this new thing. It's yesterday's when-then plan with a particular kind of when: not a time on the clock, which is easy to miss, but an action that has already proven it happens.

teach.h: MATCH THE ANCHOR TO THE HABIT.
teach.b: Fogg advises matching the anchor to the new habit: the right place, the right moment, the right frequency. A practice of stillness fits better after setting down the keys than after starting the car.
Fourth, an old pattern, with a twist on yesterday. Yesterday's psalm named times of day. This text names actions.

teach.h: WHEN THOU LIEST DOWN, WHEN THOU RISEST UP.
teach.b: In Deuteronomy, the King James Bible says: "thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children, and shalt talk of them when thou sittest in thine house, and when thou walkest by the way, and when thou liest down, and when thou risest up."
In Jewish tradition this passage is part of the Shema, said in the evening and in the morning. Sitting, walking, lying down, getting up: anchors that come around every day.
Fogg adds one modern touch: after the new habit, a small moment of celebration, a smile, a quiet yes, so the brain marks it as worth doing again.

how: People following B. J. Fogg's method attach a new habit to an existing routine with a short recipe, "after I do this, I will do that," and mark it with a small celebration; in Jewish tradition the Shema, which includes this passage, is said in the evening and the morning.

games.q: you want to add a minute of stillness to your day. which anchor do you pick?
o: after I set down my keys at home.
after I open my work email.
games.why: Fogg's advice is to match the anchor to the habit. stillness fits a moment of arriving, not of starting to drive.

practice: Settle on the breath and walk through an ordinary day, listing the things that happen no matter what: waking up, the first drink, leaving the house, coming home, brushing teeth at night.

Pick the one that best fits a moment of stillness, and fill in the sentence silently, "After I…, I will…," keeping the second half small. Say it once more, then let the breath be the only thing happening.

wordCard.voice: Habit anchors. Things you already do every day, used as the hook for a new practice: after this, that. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: after this, that. And once the new thing is done, a small nod. See you tomorrow.
